catalog_quote: Fonem suprasegmental yang ditemukan di dalam bahasa Simalungun adalah tekanan. Tekanan di dalam bahasa Simalungun dapat membedakan arti atau bersifat fonemis. Kecuali adjektiva, pada umumnya kata yang bersuku kata dua mendapat tekanan pada suku kata pertama. Meskipun demikian, kadang-kadang terjadi pemindahan tekanan ini dari suku kata pertama ke suku kata kedua, khususnya pada adjektiva yang dibentuk dari verba yang sama sehingga menyebabkan perubahan makna. Beberapa verba yang bersuku dua dan mendapatkan tekanan utama pada suku kata pertama dapat dibentuk menjadi adjektiva dengan memindahkan tekanan utama ini ke suku kata yang kedua. Kelihatannya gejala ini agak umum pada bahasa-bahasa Batak. Hal yang sama, misalnya, juga ditemukan pada bahasa Angkola (Siregar, 1996). Berikut ini diperlihatkan beberapa pasangan yang dapat menunjukkan kontras fonem suprasegmental di dalam bahasa Simalu…

new_statements.quote: Fonem suprasegmental yang ditemukan di dalam bahasa Simalungun adalah tekanan. Tekanan di dalam bahasa Simalungun dapat membedakan arti atau bersifat fonemis. Kecuali adjektiva, pada umumnya kata yang bersuku kata dua mendapat tekanan pada suku kata pertama. Meskipun demikian, kadang-kadang terjadi pemindahan tekanan ini dari suku kata pertama ke suku kata kedua, khususnya pada adjektiva yang dibentuk dari verba yang sama sehingga menyebabkan perubahan makna. [...] Kelihatannya gejala ini agak umum pada bahasa-bahasa Batak. [...] [álbak] 'memukul dengan kayu besar' / [albák] 'mengelupas'; [áyak] 'kejar' / [ayák] 'suka sekali'
new_statements.translation: The suprasegmental phoneme found in Simalungun is stress. Stress in Simalungun can distinguish meaning, i.e. it is phonemic. Except for adjectives, disyllabic words generally receive stress on the first syllable. Nevertheless, this stress is sometimes shifted from the first to the second syllable, particularly in adjectives formed from the same verb, causing a change of meaning. [...] This phenomenon seems to be fairly common in the Batak languages. [...] [álbak] 'to beat with a big stick' / [albák] 'to peel off'; [áyak] 'to chase' / [ayák] 'to like very much'
new_statements.citation: Siregar, Bahren Umar; Parlindungan Purba; Chairul Husni. 2001. Fonologi Bahasa Simalungun. Jakarta: Pusat Bahasa, Departemen Pendidikan Nasional. x+126 pp. ISBN 979-685-176-8.
new_statements.locator: Bab III, sec. 3.9 'Fonem Suprasegmental', pp. 89-90 (PDF pp. 99-100); repeated in Bab VI 'Simpulan' p. 105 (PDF p. 115); acoustic figures pp. 91-92
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (136 pp., Acrobat scanned layer; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Fonologi bahasa simalungun.tif') and the page images pages/, -, -. Printed p. 89 = PDF p. 99 (page header '89' visible), sec. 3.9 'Fonem Suprasegmental'. The quoted passage is there verbatim as printed: 'Fonem suprasegmental yang ditemukan di dalam bahasa Simalungun adalah tekanan. Tekanan di dalam bahasa Simalungun dapat membedakan arti atau bersifat fonemis. Kecuali adjektiva, pada umumnya kata yang bersuku kata dua mendapat tekanan pada suku kata pertama. Meskipun demikian, kadang-kadang terjadi pemindahan tekanan ini dari suku kata pertama ke suku kata kedua, khususnya pada adjektiva yang dibentuk dari verba yan…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the first syllable of disyllabic words (= the penult; the source discusses only disyllables, so initial vs. penult cannot be separated from this description alone), with a contrastive shift to the second/final syllable in adjectives, especially adjectives derived from verbs; the source calls stress the language's only suprasegmental phoneme and gives five minimal pairs (verb initial-stressed vs. adjective final-stressed).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the source speaks only of 'tekanan utama' (primary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: Adjectives (esp. deverbal) carry stress on the second syllable: [ádat] 'custom' vs [adát] 'select seedling', [tórop] 'a kind of tree' vs [toróp] 'medium', [déjep] 'shiny' vs [dejép] 'sharp'; word-final /k p t/ in a stressed final syllable surface as retroflex/implosive allophones (pp. 88-89). Simpulan p. 105: stress is phonemic in disyllabic words, particularly verbs and adjectives.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, elicited citation forms from the Simalungun Atas (Upper) dialect, Kecamatan Raya and Kecamatan Purba, Kabupaten Simalungun (sec. 1.5); statement covers disyllabic words only; two pairs shown with spectrogram/amplitude figures (pp. 91-92).
new_statements.identity_note: Siregar et al. 2001 describe the Simalungun Atas (Upper) dialect, data from Kecamatan Raya and Kecamatan Purba, Kabupaten Simalungun (sec. 1.5); the book names three main dialects (Atas, Tengah, Bawah). Glottolog bata1288 lists no dialect-level glottocodes; language-level bata1288 applies.

new_statements.quote: Perlu diperhatikan bahwa bila tekanan pada kedua bentuk itu berbeda, tekanan pada yang pertama jatuh pada -mu, dan pada yang kedua jatuh pada fonem kata yang dilekati oleh -m itu, seperti /bapámu/ – /bapám/ maka arti pada yang pertama lebih hormat atau sopan, sedangkan pada yang kedua kurang hormat atau kurang sopan dan sedikit agak kasar. [...] Pada kata-kata yang berfonem akhir konsonan, -mu itu tetap berbentuk -mu, tidak ada perubahan dari segi morfologis, semestinya ditentukan oleh perbedaan letak tekanan dan juga oleh hubungan kalimat. Contoh: /inaŋmu/ 'ibu anda' (nilai kata lebih hormat) /inaŋmu/ 'ibumu' (nilai kata kurang hormat)
new_statements.translation: Note that when the stress on the two forms differs, the stress in the first falls on -mu and in the second on the phoneme of the word to which -m is attached, as in /bapámu/ – /bapám/; the meaning of the first is then more respectful or polite, while the second is less respectful or less polite and somewhat coarse. [...] For words ending in a consonant, -mu keeps the form -mu; there is no morphological change, and [the distinction] should be determined by the difference in stress placement and also by the sentence context. Examples: /inaŋmu/ 'your (polite) mother' (more respectful) – /inaŋmu/ 'your mother' (less respectful).
new_statements.citation: Damanik, Urich H; Maridin Sinaga; Abu Bakar; Janiapo Purbo. 1984. Morfologi dan Sintaksis Bahasa Batak Simalungun. Jakarta: Pusat Pembinaan dan Pengembangan Bahasa. xiii+119 pp.
new_statements.locator: Bab 2, sec. 2.3.5 'Proses Morfofonemik -mu', printed p. 67 (PDF p. 78); continuation of examples p. 68 (PDF p. 79). The only other 'tekanan' hit, p. 26 (PDF p. 37), concerns emphatic particles (pe, ma, do), not word stress.
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with Siregar et al. 2001 (existing statement: stress is phonemic; disyllables generally stressed on the first syllable, with shifts to the second syllable in deverbal adjectives that change meaning). Damanik adds another meaning-bearing stress contrast, in the possessive -mu/-m forms, where the polite form is stressed on the suffix (final syllable of a trisyllable) rather than on the stem. It does not state a general placement and so neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's penultimate/initial rule; it supports the 'stress is distinctive' claim and enlarges the list of exceptions (suffix-attracted stress in honorific -mu forms).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work is a morphology-syntax survey with no phonology or stress section and states no general word-stress rule. Its one remark on word stress: in the possessive forms, the polite/honorific suffix -mu carries the stress (bapamú), whereas the familiar allomorph -m leaves the stress on the stem (bapám); for consonant-final stems the two forms are segmentally identical (inangmu 'your mother' polite vs familiar) and are told apart by stress placement and context, i.e., stress placement carries a meaning (register) distinction.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the -mu/-m register contrast; nothing on other word classes. Note the printed example marks the accent on the second syllable of both /bapámu/ and /bapám/, which does not match the prose (stress on -mu in the first form); this is either a typesetting inconsistency or a mark with a different value.
new_statements.identity_note: Damanik et al. 1984 sample the Simalungun of Pematang Raya, Kecamatan Raya, Kabupaten Simalungun (chosen as the variety least influenced by Karo, Toba Batak and Malay), with comparison notes from bus drivers in Tanah Jawa and Pematang Siantar (p. 4, PDF p. 15). Same locality as Mayani 2017's geminate data already held by the project.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources on placement, because Damanik et al. 1984 state no general rule. Two small points: (1) Damanik's polite form bapamú (stress on the suffix -mu, final syllable of a trisyllabic word) is outside the disyllabic-word generalisation of Siregar et al. 2001 (first syllable of disyllables, with exceptions), so it is an additional morphologically conditioned exception rather than a contradiction; (2) within Damanik's own page, the printed accent marks on /bapámu/ – /bapám/ both sit on the second syllable 'pa', which is inconsistent with the sentence that says the stress in the first form falls on -mu; the prose, not the diacritic, is the deciding statement.
